title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt IX: Sea-Monsters and the Queen’s Cup (lines 559–661)
part: Fitt IX · Sea-Monsters and the Queen’s Cup (lines 559–661)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 22–25, lines 559–661 (fitt IX). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Swā mec gelōme lāðgetēonan
þrēatedon þearle.
sentences.l: So me often the hateful injurers pressed hard.
sentences.i: So again and again those hateful tormentors beset me, and sorely.
sentences.n: This unit continues the speech that Beowulf began at 530 (‘Hwæt, þū worn fela …’), so Klaeber prints no opening quotation mark here. It follows his account of the sea-beast he killed at 549–558 and says that such attacks came again and again. ‘Swā’ is ‘so, in that way’. ‘mec’ is the longer accusative form of ‘ic’ (the shorter ‘mē’ serves as dative and accusative) and is the object of ‘þrēatedon’. ‘gelōme’ is ‘often’. The subject is ‘lāðgetēonan’, nominative plural of ‘lāðgetēona’, a compound of ‘lāð’, ‘hateful’, and ‘getēona’, ‘injurer’ (related to ‘tēona’, ‘harm’); the word looks to be a rare one, so ‘hostile injurers’ is partly a guess from its parts. ‘þrēatedon’ is the past plural of ‘þrēatian’, which covers ‘press hard, harass, threaten’ (the English ‘threaten’ is the same word). ‘þearle’ is the adverb ‘sorely, severely’. The injurers are the sea-monsters of the swim.

sentences.t:
Ic him þēnode
dēoran sweorde, swā hit gedēfe wæs.
sentences.l: I served them with precious sword, as it fitting was.
sentences.i: I served them with my precious sword, as was fitting.
sentences.n: ‘þēnode’ is the past of ‘þēnian’, ‘serve’, a verb that takes the dative, so ‘him’ is ‘them’ (the monsters) and ‘sweorde’ is the dative of the instrument, ‘with a sword’. ‘dēoran’ is dative singular of ‘dēore’ in the weak form (the strong dative would be ‘dēorum’), which can mean ‘dear, precious’ and also ‘stern, fierce’; I take the first and leave the second as a possibility. ‘swā hit gedēfe wæs’ is ‘as it was fitting’: ‘gedēfe’ is an adjective in the predicate, ‘suitable, becoming’, and ‘hit’ is the whole action. The verb of service is used with grim humour. Hosts serve guests, and Beowulf says he served the monsters with the sword, in the way that the next sentence will turn into a joke about a meal.

sentences.l: Not they of that fill joy had, the wicked ill-doers, that they me partook of, a feast sat around near the sea-ground;
sentences.i: They had no joy of that meal, those wicked ill-doers, in feasting on me, in sitting round their banquet near the sea floor;
sentences.n: ‘Næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’, and here it works as a plain ‘not’ before ‘hæfdon’; I take it so from the sense. ‘hīe’ is ‘they’ (the monsters), and ‘gefēan’ is the accusative, the object of ‘hæfdon’, of the weak noun ‘gefēa’, ‘joy’, and ‘ðǣre fylle’, feminine genitive (it could also be a dative), is ‘of that fill’, that is of that meal (‘fylle’ is ‘one's fill, a full meal’). ‘mānfordǣdlan’ is a nominative plural noun in apposition to ‘hīe’: ‘mān’ is ‘wickedness, crime’, and ‘fordǣdla’ is ‘evil-doer’ (a compound of ‘for-’ and ‘dǣd’, ‘deed’); I join them as ‘wicked ill-doers’, a guess at the shade. The ‘þæt’ clause says what the fill would have been: ‘þæt hīe mē þēgon’, ‘that they partook of me’. ‘þēgon’ is the past plural of ‘þicgan’, ‘receive, take, eat’ (618 has the compound ‘geþeah’ of Hrothgar taking the cup), and ‘symbel ymbsǣton’ is a second past plural, ‘sat around a feast’, with ‘symbel’ the accusative object of ‘ymbsittan’. Both end in -on, which is the indicative ending of a past plural (a subjunctive would end in -en), so the clause says what the monsters did. ‘sǣgrunde nēah’ is ‘near the sea-ground’: ‘nēah’ takes the dative. The scene is the monsters' own banquet, with Beowulf as the dish they had hoped for.

sentences.t:
ac on mergenne mēcum wunde
be ȳðlāfe uppe lǣgon,
sweo[r]dum āswefede, þæt syðþan nā
ymb brontne ford brimlīðende
lāde ne letton.
sentences.l: but in the morning, wounded by swords, by the wave-leaving up they lay, put-to-sleep by swords, so that thereafter never about the steep ford sea-travelers on their way hindered.
sentences.i: But in the morning they lay up on the shore, wounded and put to sleep by swords, so that never afterwards did they hinder seafarers on their way about the steep strait.
sentences.n: ‘on mergenne’ is a dative, ‘in the morning’ (‘mergen’ is a variant of ‘morgen’). ‘mēcum wunde’ is ‘wounded with swords’: ‘wunde’ is a plural adjective agreeing with the unstated ‘they’, and ‘mēcum’ is the dative plural of ‘mēce’, ‘sword’. ‘be ȳðlāfe’ is ‘by the wave-leaving’: ‘ȳð’ is ‘wave’ and ‘lāf’ is ‘what is left’, so this is what the waves leave behind, the shore or the tide-line, which is a guess at the exact place. ‘uppe lǣgon’ is ‘lay up’, that is on land. ‘āswefede’ is the past participle plural of ‘āswebban’, ‘put to sleep’, an old word for ‘kill’; compare ‘swefeð’ at 600. The apparatus gives ‘sweodum’ under the siglum ‘A’ (as I take it, one of the Thorkelin transcripts, not the manuscript), which gives no word. Kemble (‘Ke.’) added ‘r’, making ‘sweordum’, and Klaeber marks it ‘sweo[r]dum’, so the ‘r’ is an editorial restoration. The result clause begins ‘þæt syðþan nā … lāde ne letton’: ‘letton’ is the past plural of ‘lettan’, ‘hinder’. ‘brimlīðende’, ‘sea-travelers’ (‘brim’ is ‘sea’ and ‘līðende’ the participle of ‘līðan’, ‘to travel’), is the object of ‘letton’; the nominative and accusative plural of the participle look alike, so this is a reading from the sense. The subject of ‘letton’ is the monsters, understood from before, and ‘lāde’ is the dative of ‘lād’, ‘way, course’, ‘in their course’: ‘hindered sea-travellers in their passage’. The loose word order makes this a reading from the grammar. ‘ne … nā’ is a double negative that strengthens the denial. ‘ymb brontne ford’ is ‘around the steep ford’: ‘brontne’ is accusative of ‘bront’, ‘steep, high’. ‘ford’ is usually a shallow crossing, but with ‘brontne’ and ‘brimlīðende’ it seems to be a sea-passage or sound, which is a guess. Beowulf presents the killing as a service to sea-travellers.

sentences.t:
Lēoht ēastan cōm,
beorht bēacẹn Godes, brimu swaþredon,
þæt ic sǣnæssas gesēon mihte,
windige weallas.
sentences.l: Light from the east came, bright beacon of God, the seas subsided, so that I the sea-headlands could see, the windy walls.
sentences.i: Light came from the east, the bright beacon of God, and the seas grew calm, so that I could see the headlands, the wind-swept cliffs.
sentences.n: ‘Lēoht ēastan cōm’ is ‘light came from the east’: ‘ēastan’ is an adverb ‘from the east’. ‘beorht bēacẹn Godes’ is in apposition to ‘lēoht’, ‘bright beacon of God’, and it names the sun without using the word; a ‘bēacen’ is a sign or signal-fire. The dot under the ‘e’ in ‘bēacẹn’ is Klaeber's sign that this vowel does not count in the metre, so the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there. ‘brimu swaþredon’ is ‘the seas subsided’: ‘brimu’ is a neuter plural, ‘seas, surf’, and ‘swaþredon’ is past plural of ‘swaþrian’; ‘subside, grow calm’ is my rendering of a rare verb, and the sense is partly a guess from the context (the light comes and the waves lie down, so the headlands can be seen). The ‘þæt’ clause is a result: ‘þæt ic sǣnæssas gesēon mihte’, ‘so that I could see the sea-headlands’. ‘næss’ is a ‘ness’, a headland, the same as in English place-names such as ‘Skegness’. ‘windige weallas’ is ‘windy walls’, the cliffs along the shore, and both words are accusative plural. Beowulf's own Christian view shows here, since the poem has him say it: the sun is God's beacon, and it arrives at the end of the night's fighting.

sentences.t:
Wyrd oft nereð
unfǣgne eorl, þonne his ellen dēah!
sentences.l: Fate often saves the not-doomed earl, when his valor avails!
sentences.i: Fate often delivers a man who is not fated to die, when his valor serves!
sentences.n: A general statement in the present tense. ‘Wyrd’ is ‘fate’ (the house rendering), the subject of ‘nereð’, third person singular of ‘nerian’, ‘save, rescue’. ‘unfǣgne eorl’ is accusative: ‘fǣge’ means ‘doomed to die’ (it is the word behind Scots ‘fey’), so ‘unfǣgne’ is ‘not-doomed’, a man whose time has not come. ‘þonne his ellen dēah’ is ‘when his valor avails’: ‘þonne’ is ‘when, if’, ‘ellen’ is ‘valor’ (the house rendering, as in ‘valor-bold’), and ‘dēah’ is the third person singular of ‘dugan’, ‘be good, avail’, the verb that appears as ‘dohte’ at 526. The line gives both causes, fate that spares and valor that does the work, and puts them in one condition: fate saves the man who is not doomed if he fights well. The exclamation mark is Klaeber's.

sentences.t:
Hwæþere mē gesǣlde, þæt ic mid sweorde ofslōh
niceras nigene.
sentences.l: Yet it befell me that I with sword slew sea-monsters nine.
sentences.i: And yet it befell that I slew nine sea-monsters with my sword.
sentences.n: ‘Hwæþere’ is ‘yet’ (cf. ‘hwæþre’ at 555). ‘mē gesǣlde’ is ‘it befell me’: ‘gesǣlan’ is an impersonal verb, ‘happen, befall’, with the dative of the person, the same sense as ‘gyfeþe wearð’ at 555, that the outcome was granted. The ‘þæt’ clause then has an indicative verb, ‘ofslōh’, the past of ‘ofslēan’, ‘strike down, slay’, with ‘niceras nigene’ as the accusative object: ‘nicor’ is a water-monster, and ‘nigene’ is the accusative of ‘nigon’, ‘nine’. The apparatus shows editors unsettled here, though the meaning is not in doubt. It lists two proposals: Rieger would put ‘mēce’ (‘with a sword’) for ‘sweorde’, and Holthausen would put ‘ābrēat’ (‘killed’) for ‘ofslōh’. The apparatus gives no reasons and prints the cross-reference ‘Cf. T.C. § 28’, which I take to point to Klaeber's own textual notes (the packet does not expand ‘T.C.’). Klaeber keeps the manuscript words, and the sense is the same either way. Beowulf had said five nights on the sea at 545; the nine monsters here are told without any scene of their own.

sentences.l: Not I in night have heard, under heaven's vault, of a harder man fighting, nor on sea-streams of a more wretched man;
sentences.i: I have never heard of a sterner fighter by night beneath the vault of heaven, nor of a man more wretched on the sea-streams;
sentences.n: ‘Nō ic … gefrægn’ is ‘I have not heard (by asking)’, a formula for vouching for a report; ‘gefrægn’ is the past of ‘gefrignan’. ‘on niht’ is ‘in the night’. The construction after ‘gefrægn’ is an accusative with an infinitive, and I read ‘heardran’ as an accusative singular masculine comparative with its noun left out, ‘a harder (man)’, matching ‘earmran mannon’ (accusative singular, ‘a more wretched man’) in the second half: ‘I have not heard of a harder (man) fighting … nor of a more wretched man on the sea-streams’. That is my reading from the grammar; I cannot settle the case of ‘heardran’ from the form alone. ‘feohtan’ is the infinitive, ‘to fight’. ‘heofones hwealf’ is ‘heaven's vault’, the arch of the sky. ‘ēgstrēamum’ is dative plural, ‘on sea-streams’, with ‘ēg-’ a first element that I take to mean ‘water’; compare ‘ēagorstrēam’ at 513. ‘earm’ is the adjective ‘poor, wretched’, comparative ‘earmran’. Beowulf says that he has heard of no sterner fighter by night, and no man more wretched on the sea-streams, than he was in that fight.

sentences.t:
hwæþere ic fāra feng fēore gedīgde
sīþes wērig.
sentences.l: Yet I the foes' grasp with life survived, of the journey weary.
sentences.i: Yet I came through the grip of my enemies with my life, weary from the journey.
sentences.n: ‘hwæþere’ is ‘yet’ again, as at 574; Klaeber prints an italic ‘æ’, his sign that he changed a letter, and the apparatus says the manuscript has ‘hwaþere’ and that ‘Gru.’ prints ‘hwæþere’, with a cross-reference to ‘Tho.’ (Thorkelin) and ‘Gr.1’, so this is a matter of spelling. ‘fāra feng’ is ‘grasp of the hostile’: ‘feng’ is the accusative of ‘feng’, ‘grasp, grip’ (from ‘fōn’, ‘seize’), and ‘fāra’ is genitive plural, I take it of ‘fāh’, ‘hostile’, used as a noun, ‘of the hostile ones’; A reading ‘the grip of dangers’ would need a noun ‘fǣr’, ‘sudden danger’, whose genitive plural is written with ǣ, not with the ā that Klaeber prints, so I leave it as a possibility I cannot confirm. ‘fēore gedīgde’ is ‘survived with life’: ‘gedīgan’ is ‘come through, survive’, ‘fēore’ the dative of ‘feorh’, ‘life’; the same verb returns in the second person at 661. ‘sīþes wērig’ is ‘weary of the journey’, with ‘sīþes’ a genitive after the adjective. The line says that Beowulf came through alive but worn out; it closes his report of the night's fighting.

sentences.t:
Ðā mec sǣ oþbær,
flōd æfter faroðe on Finna land,
wadu weallendu.
sentences.l: Then me the sea bore away, flood after the current, to the Finns' land, the waters welling.
sentences.i: Then the sea carried me off, the flood following the current, to the land of the Finns, the waters surging.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā mec sǣ oþbær’ is ‘then the sea bore me away’: ‘oþbær’ is the past of ‘oþberan’, ‘carry off’, with ‘sǣ’ the subject and ‘mec’ the object. ‘flōd æfter faroðe’ is ‘flood after the current’, the flood-tide following the stream; ‘faroð’ is a poetic word for a stream or shore, and I take it as the stream, which is a guess at the shade. ‘on Finna land’ is ‘to the land of the Finns’ (genitive plural). The poem tells no more of the Finns here, so where their land lay is a guess. ‘wadu weallendu’ is ‘waters welling’, both nominative plural neuter; ‘wadu’ is the plural of ‘wæd’, ‘water, shallows’, as at 508 and 546 (there spelled ‘wada’ and ‘wado’). The manuscript has ‘wudu’, which would be ‘wood’ and does not go with ‘weallendu’; the apparatus credits ‘wadu’ to ‘Gru.tr.’ (cited as printed) and to Kemble (‘Ke.’), and Klaeber's italic ‘a’ marks that change. Beowulf's own account puts him in the land of the Finns, where Unferth's story had Breca reach the Heathoreams.

sentences.t:
Nō ic wiht fram þē
swylcra searonīða secgan hȳrde,
billa brōgan.
sentences.l: Not I a whit about you of such cunning-hatreds have heard say, the terrors of blades.
sentences.i: I have never heard anything told about you of such cunning battles, such terrors of blades.
sentences.n: ‘Nō ic wiht … hȳrde’ is ‘I have heard nothing at all’, where ‘wiht’ (‘a thing’) is either an adverb of strong denial, as at 541, or a noun, ‘nothing of’, with the genitive plural ‘swylcra searonīða’ depending on it; either way that phrase is ‘of such cunning-hatreds’: ‘searo’ is ‘skill, device, cunning’ and ‘nīð’ is ‘hatred, violence’, so ‘searonīð’ is a hostile struggle won by craft (the compound is rare, and ‘cunning-hatred’ is a literal rendering, not a settled meaning). ‘secgan hȳrde’ is ‘heard said’, with an infinitive. ‘fram þē’ is ‘from you’, and I read it as ‘concerning you’, that is, no such account ever reached him from anyone about Unferth; the other reading, that no such thing had come from Unferth himself, is possible and I cannot exclude it. ‘billa brōgan’ is ‘of blades the terror’: ‘billa’ is genitive plural of ‘bill’, ‘sword’, and ‘brōgan’ has the weak ending -an, which is accusative (singular or plural) here; I take it as plural, loosely in apposition to ‘searonīða’, and the number is my choice.

sentences.t:
Breca nǣfre gīt
æt heaðolāce, nē gehwæþer incer,
swā dēorlīce dǣd gefremede
fāgum sweordum — nō ic þæs [fela] gylpe —,
þēah ðū þīnum brōðrum tō banan wurde,
hēafodmǣgum;
sentences.l: Breca never yet at battle-play, nor either of you two, so boldly a deed performed with gleaming swords — not I of that [much] boast —, though you to your brothers to slayer became, to head-kinsmen;
sentences.i: Never yet did Breca do so bold a deed in battle with gleaming swords, nor either of you two (I do not boast much of that), though you became the slayer of your own brothers, your nearest kin;
sentences.n: The subject is ‘Breca’, and the verb ‘gefremede’ (past singular of ‘gefremman’, ‘perform’) comes after the long second subject, ‘nē gehwæþer incer’, ‘nor either of you two’. ‘incer’ is the genitive of the dual ‘git’ (see 508), so the line pairs Breca and Unferth, who told the tale, and says neither did a deed so bold. ‘æt heaðolāce’ is ‘at battle-play’, dative, with ‘lāc’ meaning ‘play, sport’. ‘dēorlīce’ is the adverb ‘boldly, fiercely’. ‘fāgum sweordum’ is dative plural, ‘with gleaming swords’; ‘fāh’ has several senses, ‘coloured, adorned, shining’ and ‘stained’, and here I take ‘gleaming’ with ‘stained’ as the other choice, a guess. The parenthesis between the dashes, ‘nō ic þæs [fela] gylpe’, is ‘I do not boast much of that’: ‘gylpe’ is first person singular of ‘gylpan’, ‘boast’, which takes the genitive, ‘þæs’. The brackets matter. The apparatus does not print the manuscript reading, but the brackets mean ‘fela’, ‘much’, is Klaeber's addition (the apparatus names ‘Gr.1’ and ‘Sed.’, that is Sedgefield, for it), and Kluge, Holthausen, Schücking and Chambers read ‘[geflites]’ instead, ‘of strife’; with that word the clause would mean ‘I do not boast of that strife’. I follow Klaeber and mark ‘[much]’ as an editorial supply. The clause after the dash, ‘þēah ðū … wurde’, is concessive: ‘wurde’ is second person singular past of ‘weorþan’ (the subjunctive, which ‘þēah’ asks for, has the same form as the indicative here), ‘become’, ‘tō banan’ is ‘as slayer’, ‘brōðrum’ is dative plural, and ‘hēafodmǣgum’ in apposition is ‘head-kinsmen’, which I take as ‘nearest kin’ (a guess; ‘hēafod’ can mean ‘chief’ and ‘mǣg’ is ‘kinsman’). The poem does not tell the story here; the charge is that Unferth killed his own brothers.

sentences.t:
þæs þū in helle scealt
werhðo drēogan, þēah þīn wit duge.
sentences.l: For that you in hell shall damnation suffer, though your wit avail.
sentences.i: For that you shall suffer damnation in hell, though your wit serve you well.
sentences.n: ‘þæs’ is a genitive of cause, ‘for that’, pointing back at the killing of the brothers. ‘þū in helle scealt werhðo drēogan’ is ‘you shall suffer damnation in hell’: ‘scealt’ is second person singular of ‘sculan’, here a flat future, ‘drēogan’ is ‘endure, suffer’, and ‘werhðo’ is the accusative of a feminine noun that I take to mean ‘damnation, curse’ (compare ‘wearg’, ‘accursed’, which may be related); the exact word is uncertain, and I take the meaning from the context. ‘þēah þīn wit duge’ is ‘though your wit avail’: ‘duge’ is the subjunctive of ‘dugan’ (see 573 and 526), concessive. Beowulf grants Unferth's cleverness and sets damnation against it. The poem lets its Geatish hero speak of hell, a Christian idea.

sentences.t:
Secge ic þē tō sōðe, sunu Ecglāfes,
þæt nǣfre Gre[n]del swā fela gryra gefremede,
atol ǣglǣca ealdre þīnum,
hȳnðo on Heorote, gif þīn hige wǣre,
sefa swā searogrim, swā þū self talast;
sentences.l: I say to you in truth, son of Ecglaf, that never Grendel so many terrors would have done, the terrible awesome one, to your chief, humiliations in Heorot, if your mind were, your spirit, as cunning-grim as you yourself claim;
sentences.i: I tell you the truth, son of Ecglaf: Grendel, that terrible fearsome one, would never have done so many terrors to your lord, such humiliations in Heorot, if your mind and spirit had been as fierce and cunning as you yourself say;
sentences.n: ‘Secge ic þē tō sōðe’ is ‘I say to you in truth’, with ‘sunu Ecglāfes’ a vocative (as in ‘wine mīn Unferð’ at 530). The ‘þæt’ clause is an unreal condition: ‘gefremede’ is a past form whose ending is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive, but the matching ‘gif’ clause makes the sense ‘would have done’: ‘gif þīn hige wǣre … swā searogrim’ is ‘if your mind were … so cunning-grim’, with ‘wǣre’ a clear past subjunctive. ‘Gre[n]del’ has a bracketed ‘n’; the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘gre del’, with a space where the ‘n’ belongs, and Thorkelin supplied the missing letter. ‘swā fela gryra’ is ‘so many terrors’, genitive plural of ‘gryre’ after ‘fela’. ‘atol ǣglǣca’ is ‘terrible awesome one’ (Grendel; the word of 159 and 425, ‘awesome one’ again). ‘ealdre þīnum’ is dative, ‘to your chief’. I take ‘ealdor’ here as ‘chief, lord’, meaning Hrothgar (compare ‘aldre þīnum’, ‘to your chief’, at 344); the same spelling can be the dative of ‘aldor’, ‘life’, and ‘þīnum’, which is dative masculine or neuter, does not decide between them, so a lord gives the better sense. ‘hȳnðo’ is the accusative plural of ‘hȳnðu’, ‘humiliations’, in apposition to ‘gryra’. ‘sefa’ is ‘spirit’, in apposition to ‘hige’. ‘searogrim’ is ‘cunning-grim’, from ‘searo’ (see 582) and ‘grim’. ‘swā þū self talast’ is ‘as you yourself reckon’, second person of ‘talian’ (see 532). The argument is that if Unferth were really the fighter he claims to be, Grendel would not have gone on killing in Heorot.

sentences.l: but he has found out that he that feud need not, the dread sword-clash of your people, greatly fear, of the Victory-Scyldings;
sentences.i: but he has learned that he need not much fear that feud, the dread sword-clash of your people, the Victory-Scyldings;
sentences.n: ‘hē hafað onfunden’ is ‘he has found out’ (perfect, with the past participle of ‘onfindan’), and the ‘þæt’ clause gives the discovery: ‘hē þā fǣhðe ne þearf … onsittan’, ‘he need not fear the feud’. ‘þearf’ is the present of ‘þurfan’, ‘need’, and ‘onsittan’ is ‘dread, fear’ with the accusative ‘fǣhðe’, ‘feud’. ‘atole ecgþræce’ is ‘the dread sword-clash’, accusative, in apposition to ‘fǣhðe’; ‘ecgþræc’ is ‘edge-onslaught’, with ‘ecg’ ‘sword-edge’. ‘ēower lēode’ and ‘Sige-Scyldinga’ depend on it as genitives: ‘of your people, of the Victory-Scyldings’. ‘ēower lēode’ is an odd form. ‘ēower’ is the genitive plural of ‘you’, and ‘lēode’ should be ‘lēoda’ if it is a genitive plural; the apparatus lists proposed forms (‘ēowerra lēoda’, ‘ēowra lēoda’, ‘ēowre lēode’), and Klaeber keeps his print. The same shape of ‘lēode’ turns up at 599, which the apparatus cross-refers to, and at 634 Klaeber himself prints the regular ‘ēowra lēoda’. I read the phrase as ‘of your people’ in every case. ‘Sige-Scyldinga’ is ‘Victory-Scyldings’, the Danes, with ‘sige-’ ‘victory’ as an epithet-prefix like ‘Beorht-’ and ‘Gār-’. Beowulf says Grendel has found out that Hrothgar's Danes offer no resistance, and so he fears nothing from them.

sentences.t:
nymeð nȳdbāde, nǣnegum ārað
lēode Deniga, ac hē lust wigeð,
swefeð ond sendeþ, secce ne wēneþ
tō Gār-Denum.
sentences.l: he takes forced-toll, spares none of the people of the Danes, but he bears lust, puts to sleep and sends, strife expects not from the Spear-Danes.
sentences.i: He exacts his toll by force and spares none of the Danish people; he takes his pleasure, he kills and sends (them off), and he expects no fight from the Spear-Danes.
sentences.n: The grammar of the first two clauses is plain: ‘nymeð’ is ‘takes’, ‘nǣnegum ārað’ is ‘spares none’ (‘ārian’, ‘spare’, takes the dative), and ‘lēode Deniga’ is ‘of the people of the Danes’, a genitive in the odd ‘lēode’ form noted at 596. ‘nȳdbāde’ is rare: ‘nȳd’ is ‘compulsion, need’ and I take ‘bāde’ to belong to a noun ‘bād’ meaning a pledge or demand, so ‘forced-toll’ (a payment exacted under compulsion) is a guess at the sense. The rest is a crux. ‘ac hē lust wigeð, swefeð ond sendeþ’ is read in many ways, and the apparatus lists them. For ‘lust wigeð’ Kemble would add ‘on’ and read the vowel long, ‘[on] lust wīgeð’ (from ‘wīgan’, ‘fight’), while Bugge's ‘[on] lust þigeð’ (‘takes with pleasure’) matches 618, where ‘hē on lust geþeah’ says the same of Hrothgar and the cup. Klaeber's ‘wigeð’ with a short vowel is the third person of ‘wegan’, ‘carry, bear’ (it is in the same family as ‘weigh’), so ‘bears lust’, ‘indulges his pleasure’; that is my reading, flagged as a guess. For ‘swefeð’ there are two verbs: ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’, and ‘swebban’, ‘put to sleep’, an old word for ‘kill’, whose participle is ‘āswefede’ at 567. ‘sendeþ’ is ‘sends’, but it has no object, which is the real difficulty. Editors replaced it: ‘scendeð’ (‘Tho.’, Thorkelin, ‘Arn.’ and ‘B.-T.’, ‘harms, shames’), ‘swefen onsendeð’ (‘Gru.’, ‘sends a dream’), ‘swendeþ’ (‘destroys’), ‘swenceþ’ (‘afflicts’), ‘swelgeþ’ (‘swallows’) and ‘serweþ’ (‘plots’). The apparatus also has ‘He.-Soc.6 swēfeð o. s.’, with a long vowel, and I do not understand its ‘o. s.’. I put ‘puts to sleep’ in the literal line and ‘kills’ in the idiomatic line, with ‘sends (them off)’ as one possible sense, and have no confidence in it. ‘secce ne wēneþ tō Gār-Denum’ is plain: ‘secce’ is ‘strife’ (the noun is ‘sacu’ or ‘sæcc’; this form serves as genitive, dative or accusative, and ‘wēnan’ takes the genitive or accusative), ‘ne wēneþ’ is ‘does not expect’, and ‘tō Gār-Denum’ is ‘from the Spear-Danes’ (dative after ‘tō’, as in ‘wēne ic tō þē’ at 525). Beowulf's point is that Grendel kills as he likes and expects no resistance.

sentences.t:
Ac ic him Gēata sceal
eafoð ond ellen ungeāra nū,
gūþe gebēodan.
sentences.l: But I to him the Geats' strength and valor shall soon now, in war, offer.
sentences.i: But now, before long, I shall offer him the strength and valor of the Geats in battle.
sentences.n: ‘Ac ic him … sceal … gebēodan’ is ‘but I shall offer to him’: ‘sceal’ is ‘shall, must’ with the infinitive ‘gebēodan’, ‘offer, present’ (it is the verb behind ‘bid’), and ‘him’ is Grendel in the dative. The things offered, ‘eafoð ond ellen’, ‘strength and valor’, are accusatives, and ‘Gēata’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the Geats’. ‘ungeāra’ is an adverb, ‘soon’ (‘geāra’ is ‘formerly’, so ‘un-geāra’ is ‘not long hence’); with ‘nū’ it reads ‘soon, now’. ‘gūþe’ is dative, ‘in war’. The apparatus records that ‘Tho.’ (Thorkelin), ‘Gr. Bibl. ii p. 414’ (with a query) and ‘Holtzm.’ cancel ‘ic’; the sense is the same without it. The verb is a grim joke on the idea of an offering: Beowulf will offer Grendel nothing but the fight.

sentences.t:
Gǣþ eft sē þe mōt
tō medo mōdig, siþþan morgenlēoht
ofer ylda bearn ōþres dōgọres,
sunne sweglwered sūþan scīneð!’
sentences.l: Goes again he who may to mead proud-minded, after the morning-light over the children of men, of the second day, the sun, sky-clad, from the south shines!’
sentences.i: Let him go proudly to the mead again, whoever may, once the morning light of the second day, the sun clothed in the sky, shines from the south over the children of men!’
sentences.n: ‘Gǣþ’ is the present of ‘gān’, ‘go’, and it sits in the place of an imperative or future: ‘let him go’ or ‘he shall go’; I give it as a command with ‘let’ in the idiomatic line and as a statement in the literal one. ‘sē þe mōt’ is ‘he who may’: ‘mōt’ is ‘may, is allowed’ (the permission sense of ‘mōtan’, not ‘must’). ‘mōdig’ agrees with ‘sē’ and is ‘proud-minded, high-spirited’. ‘tō medo’ is ‘to the mead’, the feast, in the dative. The ‘siþþan’ clause gives the time: ‘morgenlēoht’ is the subject, ‘ofer ylda bearn’ is ‘over the children of men’ (‘ylda’ is the genitive plural of ‘ylde’, ‘men’), and ‘ōþres dōgọres’ is the genitive of time, ‘of the second day’; ‘ōþer’ means ‘second’ or ‘other’, and I take it as the day after this one, which is an inference. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘dōgọres’ is the metrical sign explained at 570. ‘sunne sweglwered’ is in apposition to ‘morgenlēoht’: ‘sunne’ is feminine, and ‘sweglwered’ is ‘sky-clad’ from ‘swegl’, ‘sky’, and ‘wered’, the participle of ‘werian’, ‘clothe’; I know of no other example of the compound, and a second reading, ‘sky-host’, is possible, so ‘sky-clad’ is a guess. ‘sūþan scīneð’ is ‘shines from the south’. The closing quotation mark ends the speech that began at 530. Beowulf ends his answer by promising a morning feast after the fight, and the invitation is to any Dane who may come.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs on sālum sinces brytta
gamolfeax ond gūðrōf;
sentences.l: Then was in joys the treasure's giver, old-haired and war-bold;
sentences.i: Then the giver of treasure was glad, grey-haired and bold in war;
sentences.n: The subject is unnamed. ‘sinces brytta’ is ‘giver of treasure’: ‘sinc’ is ‘treasure’, ‘brytta’ is ‘dispenser’ (cf. the verb ‘bryttian’, ‘to share out’), and the phrase is a standard title for a king who gives rings and arms to his followers. The reader learns from the context that it is Hrothgar; the poem next names him at 613 (‘Hrōðgāres’). ‘on sālum’ is ‘in joys’, dative plural of ‘sǣl’, ‘happiness’; ‘wæs on sālum’ is ‘was in good spirits’. ‘gamolfeax’ is ‘old-haired’, meaning grey-haired. ‘gūðrōf’ is ‘war-bold’: ‘rōf’ is ‘strong, bold’, and it ends several compounds in this part (‘sigerōf’, 619). The two epithets together make Hrothgar old and still a warrior.

sentences.t:
gēoce gelȳfde
brego Beorht-Dena;
sentences.l: in help believed the ruler of the Bright-Danes;
sentences.i: the lord of the Bright-Danes trusted in help;
sentences.n: ‘gēoce’ is the dative of ‘gēoc’, ‘help’, which ‘gelȳfde’ takes, so ‘believed in help’, ‘had trust in help’. ‘gelȳfde’ is the past of ‘gelȳfan’, ‘believe, trust’ (the English ‘believe’ is the same word). ‘brego Beorht-Dena’ is ‘lord of the Bright-Danes’, genitive plural; ‘brego’ is a poetic word for ‘prince’, and ‘Beorht-Dena’ was rendered ‘Bright-Danes’ at 427. The Danes have suffered Grendel for twelve winters (147).

sentences.t:
gehȳrde on Bēowulfe
folces hyrde fæstrǣdne geþōht.
sentences.l: heard in Beowulf the people's herdsman a firm-counselled thought.
sentences.i: the shepherd of the people perceived in Beowulf a steadfast purpose.
sentences.n: ‘gehȳrde’ is ‘heard’, and with ‘on Bēowulfe’ it means ‘perceived in Beowulf’; the thing perceived is ‘fæstrǣdne geþōht’, ‘a firm-counselled thought’. ‘fæstrǣd’ is ‘firm in counsel’, from ‘fæst’ and ‘rǣd’ (‘counsel’), so the adjective says that the purpose was settled, and both adjective and noun are accusative singular. ‘folces hyrde’ is ‘herdsman of the people’, the king as shepherd (‘hyrde’ is the same word as English ‘herd’ in ‘shepherd’). The subject, ‘folces hyrde’, comes after the verb and ‘on Bēowulfe’ and before its object, and it is Hrothgar again.

sentences.t:
Ðǣr wæs hæleþa hleahtọr, hlyn swynsode,
word wǣron wynsume.
sentences.l: There was the heroes' laughter, noise made melody, words were winsome.
sentences.i: There was the laughter of heroes, the din rang pleasantly, and the talk was cheerful.
sentences.n: Three short statements joined without ‘and’. ‘hæleþa’ is the genitive plural of ‘hæleþ’, ‘hero, man’. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘hleahtọr’, ‘laughter’, is the metrical sign explained at 570. ‘hlyn swynsode’ is ‘the din made melody’: ‘hlyn’ is ‘sound’, and ‘swynsode’ is the past of ‘swynsian’, ‘make a pleasant sound, resound’ (related to ‘swinsung’, ‘melody’). ‘word wǣron wynsume’ is ‘the words were winsome’, with ‘wynsume’ ‘pleasant, joyous’ (‘wyn’ is ‘joy’). The apparatus notes that ‘Kal.’ would read ‘wynsum’ (with a query) and that ‘Tr.’ (Trautmann) strikes ‘wǣron’. These lines describe the hall after Beowulf's speech to Unferth.

sentences.t:
Ēode Wealhþēow forð,
cwēn Hrōðgāres cynna gemyndig,
grētte goldhroden guman on healle,
ond þā frēolīc wīf ful gesealde
ǣrest Ēast-Dena ēþelwearde,
bæd hine blīðne æt þǣre bēorþege,
lēodum lēofne;
sentences.l: Went Wealhtheow forth, Hrothgar's queen, mindful of kin, gold-adorned she greeted the men in the hall, and then the noble woman gave the cup first to the homeland-guardian of the East-Danes, bade him be blithe at the beer-taking, dear to the people;
sentences.i: Wealhtheow came forward, Hrothgar's queen, mindful of what was due to her kin, and gold-adorned she greeted the men in the hall; then the noble lady gave the cup first to the guardian of the East-Danes' land, and bade him be glad at the beer-feast, and dear to his people;
sentences.n: Wealhtheow, Hrothgar's queen, first appears here. ‘Ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘went’, and ‘forð’ is ‘forth’. ‘cwēn Hrōðgāres’ is ‘Hrothgar's queen’. ‘cynna gemyndig’ is ‘mindful of kin’: ‘gemyndig’ takes the genitive, and ‘cynna’ is the genitive plural of ‘cynn’, ‘kin, kind, family’; I take it to mean she knew what was due to her family or to the several ranks present, which is a guess. ‘goldhroden’ is ‘gold-adorned’ (the participle of ‘hrēodan’, ‘adorn’, as in ‘bēaghroden’ at 623). ‘grētte … guman on healle’ is ‘greeted the men in the hall’. ‘frēolīc wīf’ is ‘noble woman’, with ‘frēolīc’ ‘free-born, noble, lovely’. ‘ful gesealde ǣrest … ēþelwearde’ is ‘gave the cup first to the guardian of the homeland’; ‘ēþelwearde’ is dative, from ‘ēþel’, ‘homeland’, and ‘weard’, ‘guardian’, and it names Hrothgar; ‘Ēast-Dena’ is the genitive plural, ‘of the East-Danes’. ‘bæd hine blīðne … lēodum lēofne’ is ‘bade him blithe … dear to the people’: ‘bæd’ is the past of ‘biddan’, ‘ask, bid’, with ‘blīðne’ and ‘lēofne’ accusative adjectives agreeing with ‘hine’, so she asked him to be glad and to be dear to the people. ‘bēorþege’ is the dative of ‘bēorþegu’, ‘beer-taking’, the word of line 117. The queen gives the cup to the king first and then goes round the rest, as the next lines show.

sentences.t:
hē on lust geþeah
symbel ond seleful, sigerōf kyning.
sentences.l: he with pleasure took the feast and hall-cup, the victory-bold king.
sentences.i: The king, bold in victory, took the feast and the hall-cup gladly.
sentences.n: ‘hē on lust geþeah’ is ‘he received with pleasure’: ‘geþeah’ is the past of ‘geþicgan’, ‘receive, take’ (the root of ‘þēgon’ at 563), and ‘on lust’ is ‘with pleasure’. Bugge's proposal for 599, ‘[on] lust þigeð’, uses the same words with the same verb (see there). ‘symbel ond seleful’ is ‘feast and hall-cup’: ‘symbel’ is the formal feast and ‘seleful’ is a compound of ‘sele’, ‘hall’, and ‘ful’, ‘cup’. ‘sigerōf kyning’ is ‘victory-bold king’ (‘rōf’ as at 608).

sentences.t:
Ymbēode þā ides Helminga
duguþe ond geogoþe dǣl ǣghwylcne,
sincfato sealde, oþ þæt sǣl ālamp,
þæt hīo Bēowulfe, bēaghroden cwēn
mōde geþungen medoful ætbær;
sentences.l: Went around then the lady of the Helmings each share of the seasoned and the young, treasure-vessels gave, until the time came that she to Beowulf, the ring-adorned queen, thriven in mind, the mead-cup bore;
sentences.i: Then the lady of the Helmings went round every part of the company, veterans and youths, and gave out the treasure-vessels, until the time came for the ring-adorned queen, ripe in mind, to bring the mead-cup to Beowulf;
sentences.n: ‘Ymbēode’ is the past of ‘ymbgān’, ‘go around’. ‘ides Helminga’ is ‘lady of the Helmings’: ‘ides’ is a poetic word for a noble woman, and ‘Helminga’ is the genitive plural of ‘Helmingas’, which I take to be the family of her birth; the poem tells no more here, so that is a guess. ‘ymbēode’ takes an accusative, so ‘dǣl ǣghwylcne’, ‘each part’ (‘dǣl’ is ‘portion, share’), is what she went round, and I take ‘duguþe ond geogoþe’, ‘of the seasoned and the young’, as genitives depending on it, the pair that 160 also uses. The forms could also be datives or accusatives, giving ‘to the seasoned and the young, each share’, and the construction is loose. ‘sincfato sealde’ is ‘gave the treasure-vessels’, ‘fato’ being the accusative plural of ‘fæt’, ‘vessel’; the cups are precious. ‘oþ þæt sǣl ālamp’ is ‘until the time came’: ‘sǣl’ is ‘time, occasion’, and ‘ālamp’ is the past of ‘ālimpan’, ‘happen’. The ‘þæt’ clause that follows names the occasion, with ‘hīo’ as ‘she’, ‘Bēowulfe’ dative, ‘bēaghroden cwēn’ ‘ring-adorned queen’, ‘mōde geþungen’ ‘thriven in mind’ (the participle of ‘geþeon’, ‘thrive, excel’), and ‘medoful ætbær’ ‘bore the mead-cup to’ (past of ‘ætberan’). The queen reaches Beowulf in his turn, and ‘geþungen’ shows she is regarded as wise as well as rich.

sentences.t:
grētte Gēata lēod, Gode þancode
wīsfæst wordum þæs ðe hire se willa gelamp,
þæt hēo on ǣnigne eorl gelȳfde
fyrena frōfre.
sentences.l: She greeted the Geats' man, to God gave thanks, wise-fast in words, that to her the wish befell, that she in any earl believed for comfort against the crimes.
sentences.i: She greeted the man of the Geats and thanked God, wise in her words, that her wish had come to her, that she could put her trust in any earl for comfort against these evils.
sentences.n: ‘grētte Gēata lēod’ is ‘greeted the man of the Geats’: ‘lēod’ is a singular noun, ‘man, prince’. ‘Gode þancode’ is ‘thanked God’, with the dative, and ‘wīsfæst wordum’ is ‘wise-fast in words’, nominative singular feminine, naming Wealhtheow as ‘firm in wisdom’. ‘þæs ðe’ is ‘because, for the fact that’, the genitive pronoun with ‘ðe’. ‘hire se willa gelamp’ is ‘to her the wish befell’; ‘gelamp’ is the past of ‘gelimpan’, ‘happen’ (the root of ‘ālamp’ at 622), and ‘willa’ is ‘wish’. The ‘þæt’ clause gives the wish: ‘þæt hēo on ǣnigne eorl gelȳfde fyrena frōfre’, ‘that she could believe in any earl for comfort’. ‘gelȳfde’ is the same past form as at 608 (the ending is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive, but a wish being reported calls for ‘could’), ‘on’ takes the accusative, ‘fyrena’ is the genitive plural of ‘fyren’, ‘crime, evil’, and ‘frōfre’ is ‘comfort’, accusative. ‘fyrena frōfre’ is ‘comfort for the evils’, that is, for Grendel's outrages. A pious queen thanks God for a man in whom she can place hope, a thought she shares with the king at 608.

sentences.l: He the cup received, the slaughter-fierce warrior, from Wealhtheow, and then spoke a speech, for war eager;
sentences.i: He took the cup from Wealhtheow, that fierce fighter, and then made his speech, eager for the fight;
sentences.n: ‘Hē þæt ful geþeah’ is ‘he received the cup’, the same verb as at 618, with ‘þæt ful’ the accusative object. ‘wælrēow wiga’ is ‘slaughter-fierce warrior’: ‘wæl’ is ‘slaughter’ and ‘rēow’ is ‘fierce, wild’, so the compound describes his temper as a fighter, which is a guess at the nuance. ‘æt Wealhþeôn’ is ‘from Wealhtheow’, dative; the circumflex over the ‘o’ is Klaeber's mark for a contracted vowel in this dative form of the name. ‘ond þā gyddode’ is ‘and then he spoke’: ‘gyddode’ is the past of ‘gieddian’, ‘speak formally, make a speech’ (cf. ‘gidd’, ‘song, formal utterance’). ‘gūþe gefȳsed’ is ‘eager for war’, the participle of ‘fȳsan’, ‘impel, drive’, with the dative ‘gūþe’. He drinks and speaks. The next line introduces the speech with the usual formula.

sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The same introduction as at 529, with ‘maþelode’ rendered by the house rows (‘spoke in speech-words’, ‘spoke in formal words’), and ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’, ‘child of Ecgtheow’, in apposition to the name. In this part the formula marks his second speech: the first, begun at 530, answered Unferth, and this one answers the queen.

sentences.t:
‘Ic þæt hogode, þā ic on holm gestāh,
sǣbāt gesæt mid mīnra secga gedriht,
þæt ic ānunga ēowra lēoda
willan geworhte, oþðe on wæl crunge
fēondgrāpum fæst.
sentences.l: ‘I that resolved, when I onto the sea mounted, the sea-boat sat in with my men's company, that I wholly your people's will would work, or in the slaughter fall, in foe-grips fast.
sentences.i: ‘I resolved, when I set out on the sea and took my seat in the boat with my company of men, that I would wholly fulfill your people's wish, or fall in the slaughter, held fast in the grip of my foes.
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins the speech. ‘Ic þæt hogode’ is ‘I resolved that’: ‘hogode’ is the past of ‘hogian’, ‘think, resolve’ (related to ‘hycgan’), with ‘þæt’ looking ahead to the clause that begins at 634. ‘þā ic on holm gestāh’ is ‘when I mounted onto the sea’: ‘gestāh’ is the past of ‘gestīgan’, ‘climb, go aboard’, with ‘on holm’ ‘onto the sea’. ‘sǣbāt gesæt’ is ‘sat in the sea-boat’, with ‘gesæt’ the past of ‘gesittan’, ‘take a seat’, followed by the accusative. ‘mid mīnra secga gedriht’ is ‘with the troop of my men’: ‘mīnra’ is the genitive plural, and ‘gedriht’ is ‘company’. ‘ānunga’ is an adverb, ‘wholly, altogether’. ‘ēowra lēoda willan geworhte’ is ‘would work your people's will’: ‘ēowra lēoda’ is a regular genitive plural (compare the odd form at 596), ‘willan’ is ‘will, wish’, and ‘geworhte’ is the past of ‘gewyrcan’, ‘accomplish’ (the ending is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive; the sense is ‘would work’). ‘oþðe on wæl crunge’ is ‘or fell in the slaughter’: ‘oþðe’ is ‘or’ (also at 637), and ‘crunge’ is the past subjunctive of ‘cringan’, ‘fall in battle’. ‘fēondgrāpum fæst’ is ‘fast in foe-grips’: ‘grāp’ is ‘grasp’ (see 555), and ‘fæst’ is ‘held fast’, so he would die in the grasp of the enemy. The two outcomes, to win or to fall, are the pair that a formal vow (a ‘bēot’, see 523) sets out.

sentences.t:
Ic gefremman sceal
eorlīc ellen, oþðe endedæg
on þisse meoduhealle mīnne gebīdan!’
sentences.l: I shall perform earl-like valor, or my end-day in this mead-hall await!’
sentences.i: I shall do a deed of valor worthy of an earl, or meet my last day in this mead-hall!’
sentences.n: ‘Ic gefremman sceal’ is ‘I shall perform’: ‘sceal’ states the duty or the resolve, and ‘gefremman’ is ‘perform, carry out’. ‘eorlīc ellen’ is ‘earl-like valor’, accusative, ‘ellen’ as at 573. ‘oþðe endedæg … gebīdan’ is ‘or await my end-day’: ‘gebīdan’ is ‘wait for, experience’ with the accusative ‘endedæg’ (‘await’ in the literal line, ‘meet’ in the idiomatic line), and ‘mīnne’ is the accusative masculine ‘my’, agreeing with it. ‘on þisse meoduhealle’ is ‘in this mead-hall’, dative, ‘meoduheall’ being ‘mead-hall’. The closing quotation mark ends the speech that began at 632. He swears to do the deed or to die in this hall, and the oath names those two outcomes only.

sentences.t:
Ðām wīfe þā word wēl līcodon,
gilpcwide Gēates;
sentences.l: To the woman the words well pleased, the boast-speech of the Geat;
sentences.i: The words pleased the lady well, the Geat's boast;
sentences.n: ‘līcodon’ is the past plural of ‘līcian’, ‘please’, which takes the dative, so ‘Ðām wīfe’ is ‘to the woman’ and ‘þā word’ is the subject; ‘wēl’ is ‘well’. ‘gilpcwide Gēates’ is in apposition to ‘word’: ‘gilp’ is ‘boast’, ‘cwide’ is ‘speech’, and ‘Gēates’ is the genitive of ‘Gēat’, ‘the Geat’ (Beowulf). Beowulf's vow is called a ‘gilpcwide’, a ‘boast-speech’, and it pleases the queen; the ‘dolgilp’ (‘foolish boast’) with which Unferth charged Beowulf and Breca at 509 is the opposite, and ‘gylpe’ at 586 is the verb ‘boast’.

sentences.t:
ēode goldhroden
frēolicu folccwēn tō hire frēan sittan.
sentences.l: went gold-adorned the noble folk-queen to her lord to sit.
sentences.i: and gold-adorned, the noble queen of the people went to sit by her lord.
sentences.n: ‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘went’, with the subject ‘folccwēn’, ‘queen of the people’ (‘folc’, ‘people’, and ‘cwēn’), and the adjectives ‘goldhroden’ (see 614) and ‘frēolicu’ (nominative feminine of ‘frēolic’). ‘tō hire frēan’ is ‘to her lord’, dative, ‘frēa’ being ‘lord’, and ‘sittan’ is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to sit’. The cup-round is over and the queen goes back to the king's side.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs eft swā ǣr inne on healle
þrȳðword sprecen, ðēod on sǣlum,
sigefolca swēg, oþ þæt semninga
sunu Healfdenes sēcean wolde
ǣfenræste;
sentences.l: Then was again as before in the hall mighty-word spoken, the people in joys, the victory-folks' noise, until suddenly Healfdene's son wished to seek evening-rest;
sentences.i: Then, as before, mighty words were spoken again in the hall, the people in high spirits, the din of the triumphant host, until suddenly the son of Healfdene wished to seek his evening's rest;
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs eft swā ǣr’ is ‘then was again, as before’, and ‘wæs’ carries through the phrases that follow: ‘þrȳðword sprecen’ is ‘mighty words spoken’ (‘þrȳð’ is ‘strength’, and ‘sprecen’ is the past participle), ‘ðēod on sǣlum’ is ‘the people in joys’, and ‘sigefolca swēg’ is ‘the noise of the victory-folks’, with ‘sigefolca’ a genitive plural. ‘ðēod’ is ‘þēod’, ‘people’, with ‘ð’ for ‘þ’. Line 643 is a crux in its order: the apparatus records that Sedgefield transposes the two half-lines, and Klaeber keeps the printed order and sends the reader to a study, MPh. iii 240, which I have not seen, so the reason is unknown to me; the clauses give the same sense in either order. ‘oþ þæt semninga’ is ‘until suddenly’. ‘sunu Healfdenes’ is ‘the son of Healfdene’, Hrothgar, and ‘sēcean wolde ǣfenræste’ is ‘wished to seek evening-rest’ (the object is accusative, though the form could also be dative or genitive; ‘ǣfenræst’ is a bed for the night). The feast ends because the king wishes to sleep, and the following lines say why he leaves the hall in Beowulf's care.

sentences.t:
wiste þǣm āhlǣcan
tō þǣm hēahsele hilde geþinged,
siððan hīe sunnan lēoht gesēon meahton,
oþðe nīpende niht ofer ealle,
scaduhelma gesceapu scrīðan cwōman
wan under wolcnum.
sentences.l: he knew for the awesome one, to the high-hall, a battle appointed, since they the sun's light see could, or darkening night over all, the shadow-helms' shapes to glide came, dark under the clouds.
sentences.i: he knew that a fight had been appointed for the fearsome one at the high hall, since the light of the sun could be seen, or since, with darkening night over all, the shadow-helmed shapes came gliding, dark beneath the clouds.
sentences.n: This sentence is hard; the reading below follows Klaeber's text, and the apparatus shows editors changing it. ‘wiste’ is the past of ‘witan’, ‘know’, with Hrothgar understood as the subject. ‘þǣm āhlǣcan’ is a variant of ‘āglǣca’ (the same word as ‘ǣglǣca’, ‘awesome one’), in the dative: ‘for the awesome one’, Grendel. ‘tō þǣm hēahsele’ is ‘to the high hall’ (read as ‘at’ in the idiomatic line), ‘hēahsele’ being Heorot. ‘hilde geþinged’ is ‘a battle appointed’: ‘geþinged’ is the past participle of ‘geþingian’, ‘settle, fix by agreement’ (from ‘þing’, ‘meeting’), and ‘hilde’, ‘battle’, is its noun; the form is the same in the accusative and the dative, and I take it as accusative after ‘wiste’, ‘knew a battle appointed’. The sense is that the fight had been fixed beforehand for Grendel. Then comes the time: ‘siððan hīe sunnan lēoht gesēon meahton’, ‘since they could see the sun's light’. At 648b the apparatus lists ‘E.Sc.’, ‘Tho.’ (Thorkelin) and four editions as inserting ‘[ne]’, so that it reads ‘since they could not see the sun's light’. With ‘ne’ the sentence says the fight was fixed from the time the sun was gone, which looks like the easier meaning; without it, as Klaeber prints, the clause says ‘since they could see the sun's light’. I follow Klaeber and have no means of deciding between them. ‘oþðe’ at 649 is the second difficulty. It is the ordinary word ‘or’ (as at 635 and 637), and both the literal and the idiomatic line keep ‘or’, so the sentence names two moments side by side: since the sun's light could be seen, or since the night came gliding on. The apparatus prints ‘opðe’ for ‘Ke.’ (Kemble), others and four editions; I cannot tell from the packet how that differs from the printed ‘oþðe’, and it may be the same word in another spelling. It also gives ‘Gru.’ and ‘Gru.tr.’ ‘oð þæt’, ‘until’, which would make the night the end of a time that began with the sun's light; Klaeber does not print that. ‘nīpende niht ofer ealle’ is ‘darkening night over all’: ‘nīpende’ is the participle of ‘nīpan’, ‘grow dark’, a rare verb which fits the context and is used at 547 (‘nīpende niht’ there too); I take the phrase as standing apart from the verb, since ‘cwōman’ is plural. ‘scaduhelma gesceapu scrīðan cwōman wan under wolcnum’ is ‘the shapes of the shadow-helms came gliding, dark under the clouds’: ‘scaduhelm’ is ‘shadow-cover’ (‘helm’ is ‘covering’ as well as ‘helmet’), ‘gesceapu’ is the neuter plural of ‘gesceap’, ‘creature, shape’ (it can also mean ‘fate’), and ‘cwōman’ is the past plural of ‘cuman’, ‘come’, with the infinitive ‘scrīðan’, ‘glide’. In the idiomatic line the genitive phrase becomes an adjective, ‘shadow-helmed shapes’. I take it as a picture of dusk, which is a guess. ‘wan’ is ‘dark’. Whichever way the time-clauses are taken, the sentence says that Hrothgar knew a fight with Grendel was fixed for the hall and that darkness was coming on.

sentences.t: Werod eall ārās.
sentences.l: The troop all arose.
sentences.i: The whole company rose.
sentences.n: ‘Werod’ is a neuter noun, ‘troop, company’, the subject, and ‘ārās’ is the past singular of ‘ārīsan’, ‘arise’. The singular verb with a collective noun makes the whole hall stand at once. Presumably they rise as the king rises to go; the text says only that the company stood.

sentences.t:
[Ge]grētte þā guma ōþerne,
Hrōðgār Bēowulf, ond him hǣl ābēad,
wīnærnes geweald, ond þæt word ācwæð:
sentences.l: Greeted then the man the other, Hrothgar Beowulf, and to him health offered, the wine-hall's rule, and that word spoke:
sentences.i: Then Hrothgar greeted Beowulf, one man the other, wished him health, offered him the rule of the wine-hall, and spoke these words:
sentences.n: ‘Grētte þā guma ōþerne, Hrōðgār Bēowulf’ is ‘the man greeted the other, Hrothgar (greeted) Beowulf’: ‘guma’ (‘man’) is the subject, ‘ōþerne’ the accusative ‘other’, and the names follow in apposition to each. The initial ‘Ge-’ in ‘[Ge]grētte’ is bracketed: the apparatus says the manuscript has ‘grette’ and that ‘Gru.tr.’ reads ‘[Ge]grētte’; it adds ‘cp.’ 2516a, 1870a and 34a (Klaeber's line numbers), which also open on a prefixed verb (‘Gegrētte’, ‘Gecyste’, ‘ālēdon’). So the prefix is Klaeber's restoration, and the meaning is the same. ‘him hǣl ābēad’ is ‘offered him hail’, ‘hǣl’ being ‘health’ (the root of ‘hale’ and of the greeting ‘hail’), and ‘ābēad’ is the past of ‘ābēodan’, ‘offer, announce’. ‘wīnærnes geweald’ is ‘the wine-hall's rule’, a second object of the same verb: ‘wīnærn’ is ‘wine-hall’ (cf. ‘þrȳþærn’, 657) and ‘geweald’ is ‘power, control’. The apparatus records ‘Gr.1 heal (?)’ and ‘Cos. (in Hold.2) healle’, that is ‘hall’ in place of ‘hǣl’, which would remove the odd pairing of ‘health’ with ‘the hall's rule’; Klaeber keeps ‘hǣl’ and cites MPh. iii 240 for ‘bēodan’ with two widely different objects. ‘ond þæt word ācwæð’ is ‘and spoke that word’: ‘ācwæð’ is the past of ‘ācweþan’, ‘utter’. Hrothgar hands the hall over for the night.

sentences.t:
‘Nǣfre ic ǣnegum men ǣr ālȳfde,
siþðan ic hond ond rond hebban mihte,
ðrȳþærn Dena būton þē nū ðā.
sentences.l: ‘Never I to any man before entrusted, since I hand and shield could lift, the strength-house of the Danes, except to you just now.
sentences.i: ‘Never before have I entrusted to any man the mighty house of the Danes, since I could lift hand and shield, except to you just now.
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Hrothgar's speech. ‘Nǣfre ic ǣnegum men ǣr ālȳfde’ is ‘never before did I entrust to any man’: ‘ālȳfde’ is the past of ‘ālȳfan’, ‘allow, entrust’, and ‘ǣnegum men’ is dative. ‘siþðan ic hond ond rond hebban mihte’ is ‘since I could lift hand and shield’, that is, since he was old enough to bear arms; ‘rond’ is ‘shield’. ‘ðrȳþærn Dena’ is ‘strength-house of the Danes’, the object of ‘ālȳfde’: ‘þrȳþ’ is ‘strength’ and ‘ærn’ is ‘house’, so the compound names Heorot, the house that is the Danes' seat of power. ‘būton þē nū ðā’ is ‘except you just now’; ‘nū ðā’ is ‘just now’ or ‘now at this moment’, a strengthened ‘now’. Hrothgar offers the keeping of the hall to a man who has just arrived.

sentences.t:
Hafa nū ond geheald hūsa sēlest,
gemyne mǣrþo, mægenellen cȳð,
waca wið wrāþum!
sentences.l: Have now and hold the best of houses, remember glories, make known might-valor, watch against the hostile!
sentences.i: Take now and keep the best of houses, remember your renown, show your strength and valor, keep watch against the foe!
sentences.n: A run of imperatives, each in the singular: ‘Hafa’ (from ‘habban’, ‘have’), ‘geheald’ (‘hold, keep’), ‘gemyne’ (from ‘gemunan’, ‘remember’), ‘cȳð’ (from ‘cȳðan’, ‘make known’), and ‘waca’ (from ‘wacian’, ‘be awake, watch’). ‘hūsa sēlest’ is ‘best of houses’, the phrase of 146 and 285. ‘mǣrþo’ is the accusative plural of ‘mǣrþu’, ‘glory’ (compare the genitive plural ‘mǣrða’ at 504), here ‘your glories’, that is, the fame he has won. ‘mægenellen’ is ‘might-valor’, a compound of ‘mægen’, ‘strength’, and ‘ellen’, ‘valor’. ‘wið wrāþum’ is ‘against the hostile’, dative plural of ‘wrāþ’, ‘hostile, angry’ used as a noun. The commands are given in the order of the evening's task: take the house, remember the fame, show the strength, stay awake.

sentences.t:
Ne bið þē wilna gād,
gif þū þæt ellenweorc aldre gedīgest.’
sentences.l: Not shall be to you of wishes lack, if you that valor-work with life come through.’
sentences.i: You shall lack nothing you wish for, if you come through that deed of valor alive.’
sentences.n: ‘Ne bið þē wilna gād’ is ‘there shall not be to you a lack of wishes’: ‘bið’ is a future-pointing present, ‘þē’ is dative, ‘wilna’ is the genitive plural of ‘willa’, ‘wish’, and ‘gād’ is ‘lack’; the idiom means that nothing he wants will be wanting, so Hrothgar is promising a reward. ‘gif þū þæt ellenweorc aldre gedīgest’ is ‘if you come through that valor-work with life’: ‘ellenweorc’ is ‘valor-work’, a deed that takes courage, ‘aldre’ is the dative of ‘aldor’, ‘life’, and ‘gedīgest’ is the second person singular of ‘gedīgan’, ‘survive’ (see 578). The closing quotation mark ends Hrothgar's speech, begun at 655. The promise is conditional on Beowulf's surviving the night.
